Everything All At Once: Bill C-34 Combines Platform Duties, a Kids’ Social Media Ban, AI Chatbot Regulation, and a Powerful Digital Safety Commission Into a Risky “Trust Us” Bet - Michael Geist

The government tabled Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, earlier today, marking its third attempt at online harms legislation after the failed 2021 consultation and Bill C-63, the Online Harms Act that died on the order paper when Parliament was prorogued ahead of the 2025 election. As I wrote on the day Bill C-63 was introduced, that bill was effectively three bills in one: a defensible set of platform regulation provisions built around a duty to act responsibly and a clear list of identifiable harms, contentious Criminal Code and Canada Human Rights Act reforms, and a powerful new Digital Safety Commission with considerable regulatory discretion. My view at the time was that the contentious provisions should be removed and addressed separately, since they were certain to dominate the debate at the expense of what really mattered, namely the platform regulation piece. That is precisely how it played out as the speech provisions undermined the bill for months, and by the time the government conceded and agreed to split the bill, time ran out.

Bill C-34 suggests the government absorbed only part of the lesson. The Criminal Code and Human Rights Act provisions are gone, but in their place the government has thrown in everything else: the original Online Harms Act platform duties, an under-16 social media ban backed by mandated age verification, Bill S-209’s pornography age verification requirements, a new AI chatbot regulatory regime, and sweeping powers for a Digital Safety Commission that will write the rules, enforce them, and decide which platforms escape the ban restriction. It is an everything-all-at-once approach in which nearly every key component, including which services face the restriction, how age gets verified, which AI systems are covered, and what standards govern exemptions, is left to regulations that do not yet exist.

I’ve been working on this piece since before the bill was introduced with the expectation that many provisions from the prior proposal would resurface. This post is long, but seeks to provide a very initial review of key elements in the bill. For those looking for the key takeaways, there are five. First, the platform regulation elements with a duty to act responsibly once again offers a good starting point for working through regulation. Second, the inclusion of a social media ban for those under 16 is bad policy that will take considerable time to implement and raises serious privacy concerns that will affect tens of millions of Canadians. Third, the AI chatbot regulations are consistent with emerging standards, but the uncertainty of who it covers is not. Fourth, the government is creating a bureaucracy comparable to the CRTC in the Digital Safety Commission as it will wield serious power and be tasked with fleshing out much of the detail of how the law will work. Fifth, the uncertainty of this bill has the hallmarks of a government wanting to do something quickly, but the “trust us” approach likely means years of implementation work and potential court challenges.

**The Foundation: A Duty to Act Responsibly**

The aspect that attracted the broadest support in Bill C-63, namely the platform regulation rules, survived largely intact. The bill features the same seven categories of harmful content (intimate content communicated without consent, content that sexually victimizes a child or revictimizes a survivor, content that induces a child to harm themselves, content used to bully a child, content that foments hatred, content that incites violence, and terrorism or violent extremism content) and revives the duty to act responsibly that requires platforms to assess and mitigate the risk of exposure to that content. There is also a duty to make certain categories of content inaccessible within 24 hours backed by a complaint path to the new Digital Safety Commission, and a duty to be transparent through public digital safety plans, record-keeping, and researcher access to data. These measures target how platforms actually operate and provide a credible starting point.

The bill also adds a synthetic content labelling obligation that requires social media services to label deepfakes and bot-amplified harmful content, a useful transparency-focused measure. The terrorism and violent extremism definition has been broadened from Bill C-63’s incitement-focused version to cover recruitment, training, facilitation, and financing. And notably, the government resisted the post-Tumbler Ridge pressure for mandatory police reporting. As I argued in the Globe and Mail in March, requiring AI companies to report users’ private conversations to police would undermine privacy and encourage corporate surveillance, and the better approach was mandated transparency about corporate reporting policies. That is what the bill does: digital safety plans must disclose “the criteria and processes, if any, that the operator applies to determine if the Royal Canadian Mounted Police – or another law enforcement agency – should be notified” of content suggesting a risk of death or serious bodily harm, along with the number of notifications made and the circumstances. There is also a five-year statutory review that will assess those measures and recommend “whether an obligation should be imposed on operators to notify a law enforcement agency.” The government’s approach is to improve transparency now and consider whether it is sufficient later."

# Blockchain Online Safety and Canada’s Sweeping Bill C-34

Amid a complex new proposal for **Blockchain online safety**, Canada has introduced its third and most ambitious attempt at regulating digital platforms, Bill C-34, also known as the Safe Social Media Act. This move coincides with growing calls to leverage blockchain technology as a foundational element for secure digital identities, a concept championed in a recent [Hill Times opinion piece](https://www.hilltimes.com/2026/06/15/put-blockchain-to-work-in-protecting-people-online/508228/). As the government seeks to establish a powerful new commission to oversee the digital space, the debate intensifies over the best way to protect citizens online.

## Canada's New Digital Strategy Takes Shape

Canada’s latest legislative effort, Bill C-34, marks a significant turning point in the country's approach to online harms. It’s a comprehensive package that bundles platform duties, a ban on social media for users under 16, and regulations for AI chatbots under one massive legislative umbrella. This "everything-all-at-once" strategy, as noted by law professor [Michael Geist](https://www.michaelgeist.ca/2026/06/everything-all-at-once-bill-c-34-combines-platform-duties-a-kids-social-media-ban-ai-chatbot-regulation-and-a-powerful-digital-safety-commission-into-a-risky-trust-us-bet/), signals the government's urgency but also raises questions about implementation and oversight.

The core of the bill establishes a "duty to act responsibly," requiring platforms to mitigate risks associated with seven categories of harmful content, including child exploitation, bullying, and incitement to violence. Platforms must make certain content inaccessible within 24 hours and provide transparency through public digital safety plans. This framework provides a credible, if challenging, starting point for holding large tech companies accountable for the content they host and amplify.

## Bill C-34: A Multi-Faceted Approach to Online Harms

The bill’s expansive scope is its most defining and controversial feature. It attempts to solve several distinct problems simultaneously, leading to a complex and potentially unwieldy regulatory structure that leaves many critical details to be determined later.

### A Contentious Mix of Regulations

Bill C-34 combines the platform duties from the previous Bill C-63 with new, highly contentious measures. The most notable is a near-total ban on social media access for individuals under 16, which will necessitate widespread age verification systems. This requirement raises significant privacy concerns for millions of Canadians, as the methods for verifying age are not specified and could lead to the collection of sensitive personal data on a massive scale. The bill also incorporates pornography age verification rules from a separate Senate bill, S-209.

### The New Digital Safety Commission

To enforce these new rules, the bill creates the Digital Safety Commission of Canada. This new body will possess powers comparable to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC), one of Canada’s most powerful regulators. The Commission will be responsible for creating the detailed regulations, enforcing them, and deciding which platforms may receive exemptions from certain rules. This concentration of power in a single entity that will both write and enforce the rules is a significant bet on bureaucratic oversight.

### Deepfakes and AI Chatbots in the Crosshairs

The legislation also introduces new obligations for services to label synthetic content, such as deepfakes and bot-amplified posts. For AI chatbots, the bill establishes a regulatory regime consistent with emerging global standards, including duties to interrupt and refer users in specific harmful situations. However, a critical ambiguity remains: the bill does not clearly define which AI systems fall under its jurisdiction, creating uncertainty for developers and operators.

## Blockchain as the Unlikely Hero for Digital ID

While the government focuses on top-down platform regulation, some argue that a more fundamental, technology-based solution is being overlooked. The concept of using blockchain for a secure and portable digital identity is gaining traction as a direct answer to the problems of anonymity, bots, and online abuse.

### The Case for a Secure Digital Identifier

An opinion piece in The Hill Times argues that blockchain technology is "an obvious part of the solution to the digital morass." Its inherent properties of strong encryption, portability, and permanence make it an ideal candidate for creating digital identifiers that are both secure and user-controlled. Such an identifier could be used to verify a person's identity without revealing unnecessary personal information, striking a balance between accountability and privacy. This approach shifts the focus from content moderation to identity verification.

### From Bot Farms to National Security

The call for secure digital IDs is not new. A previous column from October 2025 argued that every NATO country should mandate secure digital identifiers to combat the threat of online bot farms, framing the issue as a matter of national security. By requiring verified identities to post content, platforms could drastically reduce the impact of coordinated disinformation campaigns that rely on armies of anonymous accounts. This would tackle a root cause of online toxicity and manipulation.

## Conclusion

Canada's Bill C-34 represents a forceful, top-down effort to address online harms by imposing significant duties on platforms and creating a powerful new regulator. While its goal of promoting **Blockchain online safety** is clear, the bill's "trust us" approach leaves critical details on age verification, AI regulation, and enforcement to a future commission. At the same time, a parallel argument is building for a more foundational solution: leveraging blockchain to create secure, user-centric digital identities that could fundamentally change the dynamics of online interaction by mitigating anonymity-fueled abuse and disinformation.

## FAQs
**1. What is Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act?**

Bill C-34 is Canada's third attempt at online harms legislation. It combines duties for social media platforms to act responsibly, a social media ban for users under 16, AI chatbot regulations, and pornography age verification into a single, comprehensive bill enforced by a new Digital Safety Commission.

**2. How does blockchain fit into the online safety discussion?**

Advocates propose using blockchain to create a secure, portable, and permanent digital identifier for every citizen. This would allow platforms to verify user identity to combat bots and anonymous abuse, framing online safety as an identity issue rather than just a content moderation problem.

**3. What is the Digital Safety Commission of Canada?**

The Digital Safety Commission is a powerful new regulatory body proposed in Bill C-34. It will be responsible for creating specific rules based on the bill's framework, enforcing them, and hearing complaints. Its powers would be comparable to the CRTC.

**4. What are the main criticisms of Bill C-34?**

Critics argue the bill is too broad, combining too many different regulations into one package. Major concerns include the privacy implications of mandatory age verification for tens of millions of Canadians and the vast, undefined powers granted to the new Digital Safety Commission.

**5. Does Bill C-34 mandate police reporting for harmful content?**

No, the bill does not mandate that companies report users to the police. Instead, it requires platforms to be transparent in their digital safety plans about what criteria, if any, they use to notify law enforcement of potential risks. A statutory review in five years will assess if this approach is sufficient.
